claims.text: Pre-exposure untreated Q235 steel has a native oxide film and its inherent microstructure remains intact.
The native oxide film acts as a protective barrier under moderate conditions.
Elevated temperature destabilizes the native oxide film through thermal stress.
Destabilization of the native oxide film permits increased chloride penetration.
Increased chloride penetration accelerates corrosion of untreated Q235 steel.
Temperature can be isolated by comparing untreated Q235 steel at approximately 25°C and 70–100°C while holding the chloride concentration at 3.5 wt% NaCl.
The integrity and adherence of the native oxide film is the structural mediator governing corrosion onset.
At room temperature, a stable native oxide film inhibits chloride ingress and suppresses corrosion.
At elevated temperatures, thermal expansion and stress cause microcracking or spallation of the native oxide film.
Microcracking or spallation exposes the steel substrate to corrosive attack.
At fixed chloride exposure, untreated Q235 steel at 70–100°C will have a higher corrosion rate than untreated Q235 steel at approximately 25°C.
Elevated-temperature exposure will produce greater weight loss and more pronounced surface pitting than room-temperature exposure.
Under low-chloride, room-temperature conditions, the native oxide remains intact and corrosion is minimal.
Controlled chloride environments are applicable to coastal or industrial exposure settings.
The mechanism may not apply under extremely low humidity, with other aggressive species, or in entirely nonaqueous environments.
The temperature and chloride-concentration thresholds for destabilizing the native oxide are not specified and may depend on pH, exposure duration, and oxide composition.
Prior work investigated corrosion behavior in 3.5 wt% NaCl for a (CoCrFeNi)95Nb5 high-entropy-alloy coating deposited on a Q235 steel substrate.
Failure to observe both oxide-film degradation and increased corrosion at elevated temperature under chloride-rich conditions would falsify the proposed thermal-destabilization mechanism.
